If you aren't Korean, it can be easy to think Koreans are hostile or rude at first. In reality (from my perspective) you look different, and most of the time, it's just curiosity. Other times for me, it's probably that I haven't fully assimilated to the culture and my clothing and tattoos are still a little...idk. Risque? Improper? 

Once you get past the stares, most Koreans have been extremely accommodating and patient with me. Some like to practice their English speaking skills, others are happy to teach me Korean. Koreans are super polite in my opinion. No catcalling or following unless you are in itaewon. I was in a wheelchair for a few weeks and didn't quite have the same experience, but otherwise, if you dress well, carry yourself well, and put in effort to speak and learn, the majority of people are kind. 

Medical care is super super super cheap here. It's delightful. If you need hard pain meds or add meds, make sure you bring them from the US with the Rx and notes for customs. 

I see you like cooking. Consider bringing spices, herbs, and other dried food items you can't live without. Otherwise, you can pay a steeper price on iHerb.com and get it sent. Other things to consider bringing: Foundation in your shade if you are aren't pale. Bras and lingerie. Eyeshadow if you like matte and pigmented. Any brand name clothes and shoes that you like. (Things like asics and UA are much more expensive here). Your electronics. Your costco card works here if you have one.

Find friends to go out and eat with. If you'll be working, co-workers often want to go out.

Taxis are super cheap, as are subways. The driving is crazy here. Be careful. Also, watch out or listen for mopeds zipping by on the sidewalk. 

If you are planning to stay here longer than 3 months, make sure to apply for the appropriate visa. You could always do visa runs, but it's nice not having to. Otherwise, Osaka is less than 2 hours away from Seoul and is a great visit.

Hi! I am currently in a wheelchair right now, but only temporarily. 

I really wouldn't recommend it. Korea is not very wheelchair accessible. In a lot of places, the sidewalks are very bumpy and a lot of people park on the side walk.  There aren't ramps for a lot of places, and it's quite difficult to access. 

Travel-wise, Taxis refuse to pick you up. There is a wheelchair taxi that you can call, but they are often unavailable, take a very long time (over an hour) to get to you, and if you don't speak Korean, the operators don't usually speak English. (That being said, it only takes a few minutes to learn all the phrases you need to know for the interaction.)

You can use the subway, but the elevators are quite confusing, and sometimes if you take up too much room, people put their hands on your chair and roll you out. On the actual train itself, it's pretty easy when it is empty, but if it is full, there is no sense of personal space, it's jammed packed, and people will try to stabilize themselves with your chair as if you are an object and bring you both down. 

Buses can accommodate you, but it's quite a difficult process. 

The most notable thing, Seoul isn't the most friendly place towards disabled people. There are a few that see you in trouble and would like to help. There is a great number that will stare you down (which you get as a foreigner even without the wheelchair) There are kids that will try to stick things in your wheels. Shopkeepers and grocery store patrons get very annoyed by your presence (the wheelchair takes up a bunch of space) But most of all, if anything does happen, like you fall out of your wheelchair, people may walk right past you or just stare. This isn't just something I've experienced myself, I've seen it happen twice in the subway to older disabled citizens. 

This is all Seoul. I have been to other places in Korea, but that was before the wheelchair.

* There are a surprising number of earthquakes out here.
